Let’s explore Chapter Four: How Cultures and History Shape Our Approach to Death.
The way we respond to death isn’t just about biology—it’s deeply shaped by our culture and history. All around the world, people have come up with an incredible variety of rituals and beliefs to care for those who’ve passed. Some might feel familiar, like funerals, burials, or cremations. But others? They can seem almost otherworldly if you’re not from that place.
Picture this: in one community, family members come together to gently wash and dress their loved one’s body. For them, it’s a final act of love and respect. In another part of the world, people let the dead rest in the open, exposed to the wind and rain, returning naturally to the earth. It might sound strange at first, but when you see it through their eyes, it’s a beautiful tradition that carries deep meaning.
There’s a story of a traveler visiting a remote village, where instead of burying the dead, people placed them on raised platforms to decompose out in the open air. At first, the traveler was shocked. But over time, they came to understand the deep reverence behind this practice—it was all about honoring the body and letting it return to the earth in its own way.
Meanwhile, in many Western cultures, we’ve built elaborate systems that keep death at a distance. Bodies are embalmed, caskets are sealed tight, and funerals often feel formal and carefully managed. One mortician noticed that families sometimes felt left out, unsure of what was happening behind the scenes.
Still, even in these traditions, there’s room for personal choices. Some families decide to hold home funerals, caring for the body themselves in the intimacy of their own space. Others choose green burials, hoping to have a lighter impact on the environment. The mortician remembered a family who, after learning their options, skipped embalming and buried their loved one wrapped simply in a shroud. It wasn’t what everyone else did, but for them, it brought a sense of peace and comfort.
When we look back in history, we see that attitudes toward death have always evolved. Not so long ago, it was normal for families to keep the body at home for days, so friends and neighbors could come by and say goodbye. As death became more medicalized, these traditions faded away. But the mortician noticed that many people miss that closeness, even if they’re not sure how to find it again.
Religion, too, plays a huge part. Some faiths ask for burial within a certain time, others require special rituals. The mortician often worked with families from all sorts of backgrounds, each with their own needs and expectations. By honoring these customs, she helped families find meaning—even in the hardest moments.
When you step back and look at all these different ways people honor the dead, it’s clear: there’s no single “right” answer. What matters most is that the process fits the values and beliefs of those involved. The mortician saw again and again that when families were given choices, they felt more empowered—and just a little less afraid.
